In Lab 3: we build a meter for LLM calls and cost, then try prompt chaining (top row) and ReAct (middle row) on two tasks.

Task A, summarize PatchTST in three points: the chain is right every round with 2 LLM calls; ReAct is right too but uses 3 calls and costs about 3× as much, so we stop at the top row.
Task B, papers from 2023 on that learners rated ≥ 4.5: the chain is wrong every round, and silently, because it reads only the first result; ReAct is right every round, so we move down a row.

The chain’s first step uses structured output (principle ⑤).







ImportantPatterns compose, but know when to stop



One planning agent may use chaining for each step, an evaluator-optimizer for review, and routing to dispatch subtasks. But the textbook ends with this: the art is knowing when to stop adding layers.

    {"id": "P09", "title": "Attention is all you need", "year": 2017},
    {"id": "P10", "title": "BERT: pre-training of deep bidirectional transformers", "year": 2019},
    {"id": "P11", "title": "Temporal fusion transformers for interpretable time series forecasting", "year": 2019},
    {"id": "P12", "title": "Moirai: unified training of universal time series forecasting transformers", "year": 2024},
]
STOP = {"with", "from", "paper", "papers", "model", "models", "using", "published", "since", "research", "about"}

def find_papers(query, year_from=0, library=PAPERS):
    words = [w for w in query.lower().replace("-", " ").split() if len(w) > 3 and w not in STOP]
    return [p for p in library
            if p["year"] >= year_from and any(w in p["title"].lower().replace("-", " ") for w in words)]
SYSTEM = "You are the Cogito Learn paper-search assistant. Always use tools to get real data; never answer from memory."
USAGE = {"in": 0, "out": 0}

def run_agent(question, tools, run_tool, max_steps=6, show=True):
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": question}]
    calls = []
    for step in range(max_steps):
        reply = client.chat.completions.create(model=MODEL, extra_body=EXTRA, messages=messages, tools=tools)
        USAGE["in"] += reply.usage.prompt_tokens
        USAGE["out"] += reply.usage.completion_tokens
        msg = reply.choices[0].message
        messages.append(msg.model_dump(exclude_none=True))
        if not msg.tool_calls:
            return msg.content, calls
        for call in msg.tool_calls:
            args = json.loads(call.function.arguments)
            result = run_tool(call.function.name, args)
            calls.append({"args": args, "result": result})
            if show:
                print(f"🔧 {call.function.name}({args}) → {str(result)[:90]}")
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id,
                             "content": json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False)})
    return "stopped: step limit reached", calls

Summary







Principle
What we saw in the lab




③ good tools
search(q, n) → the model passed n=10 (guessing it was a result count) · search_papers(query, year_from) + descriptions → year_from=2023 every round


③ good errors
"Error" → the model rewrote its query, called again and suggested the user change their query · an error that states the cause → one call, and a plain answer to the user


④ retry
retry only temporary errors, waiting 1 → 2 seconds · the model never knew it failed


④ graceful degradation
answer from the library copy · warnings the user must see are attached by the harness, not left to the model

def run_agent(question, max_steps=6):
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": question}]
    trace = []
    for step in range(1, max_steps + 1):
        t0 = time.time()
        reply = client.chat.completions.create(model=MODEL, extra_body=EXTRA, messages=messages, tools=TOOLS)
        msg = reply.choices[0].message
        messages.append(msg.model_dump(exclude_none=True))
        trace.append({"step": step, "kind": "llm", "sec": round(time.time() - t0, 1),
                      "tokens": reply.usage.total_tokens,
                      "tools": [c.function.name for c in msg.tool_calls or []], "text": msg.content})
        if not msg.tool_calls:
            return msg.content, trace
        for call in msg.tool_calls:
            args = json.loads(call.function.arguments)
            result = run_tool(call.function.name, args)
            trace.append({"step": step, "kind": "tool", "name": call.function.name, "args": args, "result": result})
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id,
                             "content": json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False)})
    return "stopped: step limit reached", trace



def show_trace(trace):
    for t in trace:
        if t["kind"] == "llm":
            what = f"asks for tool {t['tools']}" if t["tools"] else f"answers: {t['text'][:70]!r}"
            print(f"step {t['step']} 🧠 LLM ({t['sec']} s, {t['tokens']} tokens) → {what}")
        else:
            ids = [p["id"] for p in t["result"]]
            print(f"step {t['step']} 🔧 {t['name']}({t['args']}) → {len(ids)} papers {ids}")

def react(question, max_steps=8):
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": question}]
    for step in range(max_steps):
        msg = llm(messages=messages, tools=TOOLS)
        messages.append(msg.model_dump(exclude_none=True))
        if not msg.tool_calls:
            return msg.content
        # ✏️ TODO 3 (▶ video 3:35): Run the tool the model asked for, and count the tool call
        for call in msg.tool_calls:
            result = ___
            STATS["tools"] += 1
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id,
                             "content": json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False)})
    return "stopped: step limit reached"

def react(question, max_steps=8):
    messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}, {"role": "user", "content": question}]
    for step in range(max_steps):
        msg = llm(messages=messages, tools=TOOLS)
        messages.append(msg.model_dump(exclude_none=True))
        if not msg.tool_calls:
            return msg.content
        for call in msg.tool_calls:
            result = run_tool(call.function.name, json.loads(call.function.arguments))
            STATS["tools"] += 1
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id,
                             "content": json.dumps(result, ensure_ascii=False)})
    return "stopped: step limit reached"

title: EP07 Context Window Management
section: The agent that forgot its first instruction
text:
The agent that forgot its first instruction
Picture this: we’ve been talking with a research assistant agent since nine in the morning. Our very first message said clearly: “Answer in Thai, and cite a paper every time.” Along the way we pasted in papers one by one, twelve of them. By eleven the agent answers in English, with no citations at all. The strange part: the log doesn’t show a single error. This episode explains what happened, and what the harness must do so it never happens again.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
31  EP07 Context Window Management

title: EP07 Context Window Management
text:
The agent harness
The textbook calls the structure wrapped around an LLM the agent harness. It turns the model from a text completer that remembers nothing into an agent with goals, many steps and tools (Roitman 2026, sec. 18.1). The model on its own is just a function from tokens to tokens: no memory, no API calls, no sense of time. So the textbook compares the harness to an operating system that gives the model a body.
The work splits cleanly. The thinking is the model’s; the harness handles tool calls, memory, message passing and logging every step. In our research assistant, Gemma does the thinking, but the harness calls search_papers, keeps the conversation and keeps the trace (EP06). The first piece of memory the harness must manage is the context window.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
31  EP07 Context Window Management

title: EP07 Context Window Management
section: The context window is a desk
text:
The context window is a desk
The context window is the agent’s working memory. Think of a desk: the model can read only the papers on the desk. A paper that isn’t on it, however important, is invisible to the model. And every paper on the desk has a cost: every token sent costs money and adds waiting time. Deciding what goes on the desk is one of the most consequential engineering decisions in agent design (Roitman 2026, sec. 18.2).
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
31  EP07 Context Window Management

title: EP07 Context Window Management
text:
The context budget
The textbook writes the desk’s budget as one equation. The maximum context length \(C\) must hold five parts:
\[
C \;\geq\; S + M + T + H + R
\tag{31.1}\]



Table 31.1: Five parts share one context window





Part
What it is
In our research assistant




\(S\)
system prompt
“Answer in Thai, cite a paper every time”


\(M\)
memory or retrieved data (RAG)
saved paper notes


\(T\)
tool definitions
the schema of search_papers


\(H\)
conversation history
every message since nine o’clock


\(R\)
space reserved for the answer
10% of \(C\) (in Lab 1)






The problem: \(C\) is fixed, but \(H\) keeps growing, and sometimes a tool returns a huge result at once, like a whole web page. The first approach is a fixed budget, like splitting a salary into envelopes. The textbook’s example: \(S\) 10%, \(M\) 20%, \(T\) 10%, \(H\) 50% and \(R\) 10%. Simple and predictable, but it wastes space when an envelope isn’t full. The other approach is a dynamic split every turn, which in practice means filling the most important parts first, then compressing or cutting the less important ones.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
31  EP07 Context Window Management

title: EP07 Context Window Management
text:
The silent truncation trap
Many APIs, given input longer than the context, quietly drop part of it, from the middle or from the beginning. The textbook calls this silent truncation. The system prompt may be lost, earlier instructions forgotten, or the model may hallucinate from the missing data, with no error signal at all. In our research assistant, the first message, the one saying “answer in Thai and cite papers”, is exactly what was cut.






ImportantThe textbook’s rule



Count tokens before every call, and handle overflow explicitly. Never let the API decide for you.



In Lab 1: we sent a conversation of about 270,000 tokens three ways. The pre-flight check stopped it before sending; sending it as is gave a clear 400 error; but OpenRouter’s middle-out option came back normally, 200 OK, while over 90,000 tokens from the middle were gone, so the model said there was no due date in the data. The harness caught it by comparing its own count before sending with the number of tokens the API said it really saw.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
31  EP07 Context Window Management

title: EP07 Context Window Management
text:
Compress the history ① summarize
When the history outgrows its budget, the harness must shorten it without losing what matters. The first approach summarizes the oldest \(k\) messages into one paragraph, placed before the recent messages, which stay word for word:
\[
H' \;=\; \text{Summarize}(H_{1:k}) \,\|\, H_{k+1:n}
\tag{31.2}\]
Like not replaying a week of lecture recordings, but reading a one-page summary. The first ten messages of our research assistant might become “The user studies transformers for time series, wants answers in Thai with citations, and has read two papers.” The textbook says a summary is usually 5–10× shorter than the original, and a smaller, cheaper model can do the summarizing.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
31  EP07 Context Window Management

title: EP07 Context Window Management
section: Compress the history ② keep what matters
text:
Compress the history ② keep what matters
The second approach doesn’t summarize; it chooses what to keep. The textbook offers two ways:

Selective retention: score each message by its relevance to the current question plus its recency, and keep the top \(k\). Measuring relevance needs tools we’ll meet in the RAG episodes.
Importance-weighted truncation: give each message a weight \(w_i\) (user corrections and tool results weigh more, small talk less) and keep the set with the largest total weight that fits the budget:

\[
\max_{\mathcal{K}} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{K}} w_i \quad \text{subject to} \quad \sum_{i \in \mathcal{K}} |m_i| \leq B_H
\tag{31.3}\]
Like packing a suitcase with a 20 kg limit: what’s most worth its weight goes in first. The textbook says this is a 0/1 knapsack problem, solved greedily by sorting messages by \(w_i / |m_i|\).
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
31  EP07 Context Window Management

title: EP07 Context Window Management
text:
Three sliding windows
Looking at the whole window, the textbook compares three approaches:



Table 31.2: Three sliding windows (adapted from Figure 18.2)











Approach
How
Like
Weak spot




FIFO
when full, drop the oldest message
a full whiteboard erased from the top
the first message, usually the task, goes first


Pinned + importance
pin the system prompt and the user’s first message; choose the rest by score
a sticky note with the task in the board’s corner
helps only messages known in advance to matter


Hierarchical summary
recent messages word for word, older ones as paragraph summaries, the oldest as one abstract
a pyramid of summaries
extra model calls to summarize







In Lab 2: one conversation, a 400-token budget, four methods. FIFO dropped both the task and the correction, so the answer included older papers the user had excluded. Pinning saved the task, but the later correction was still lost. Importance weights kept every instruction, but one long note didn’t fit: 5 of 6. Summarizing the old part, from 532 tokens to 156, got all 6, like the full history, with less than half the tokens.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
31  EP07 Context Window Management

title: EP07 Context Window Management
text:
Recursive context decomposition
Every method so far accepts the same constraint: everything must fit in one window. The textbook describes an idea that rejects it: a recursive language model (RLM), where the model calls itself on one part of the data at a time (Roitman 2026, sec. 18.2.5).







flowchart TB
  R["RLM(q, C)<br/>split + sub-questions"] --> A["RLM(q₁, C₁)"]
  R --> B["RLM(q₂, C₂)<br/>still big → split again"]
  R --> D["RLM(q₃, C₃)"]
  A & B & D --> F["combine → answer"]




Figure 31.1: The root splits the context, calls itself on each chunk and combines the results; no call sees the full context (adapted from Figure 18.3)





Like a lecturer facing a six-hundred-page thesis who has each teaching assistant summarize one chapter, then combines their notes. Why does it help? The textbook’s answer is context rot: a model’s accuracy drops as the context grows, even with a 128K-token window. Keeping each call short and focused avoids it. The textbook cites research where a recursive GPT-5-mini beat plain GPT-5 on difficult long-context benchmarks, while being cheaper per query.

In Lab 3: a research group’s meeting notes for a whole year, 52 weeks and 8,243 tokens, hide three decisions to drop a paper. We set a budget of 1,500 tokens per call (an assumption for this lab; the document would fit Gemma’s real window). Cutting it to fit and sending once saw only the start and found just one decision. The textbook’s recursive_summarize built a tree two levels deep, 15 calls, the largest 798 tokens, never over budget. But in the first run P04 had no week, every time, because the sub-chunks had no ## Week 27 heading line. Carrying the heading into every chunk found all three with their weeks. Each small chunk must make sense on its own.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
31  EP07 Context Window Management

title: EP07 Context Window Management
text:
Pre-flight token check
Before every LLM call the harness runs a four-item checklist, like a pilot’s checklist before take-off (Roitman 2026, sec. 18.2.6):







flowchart TB
  A["① count the prompt's tokens<br/>with the model's tokenizer"] --> B{"② prompt ≤ C − R ?"}
  B -- "fits" --> D["✅ send + ④ log tokens per part"]
  B -- "over" --> C["③ compress / cut<br/>or stop with a clear error"]




Figure 31.2: The pre-flight token check before every LLM call





Item ④ shows what takes up the space. The textbook also warns that the “4 characters ≈ 1 token” rule can be off by 20–40% for code, JSON and languages other than English, Thai included.

In Lab 1: against Gemma’s tokenizer, the four-character rule guessed 19% too many for English, but too few for Thai (32%), Python (28%) and JSON (58%). Counting with Gemma’s tokenizer, chat format included, we counted 214 and the API counted 215: one token apart.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
31  EP07 Context Window Management

title: EP07 Context Window Management
text:
Prompt architecture
The textbook says the prompt is the main channel through which the harness talks to the model: it should be modular, composable and versioned (Roitman 2026, sec. 18.3). A production system prompt usually has four sections, identity, capabilities, constraints and output format, with blanks filled in at run time, such as the agent’s name, the tool list or today’s date.
The harness doesn’t keep the prompt as one block of text; it assembles it fresh every call from five blocks:
\[
\text{Prompt} \;=\; \text{Concat}(\text{System},\ \text{Memory},\ \text{Tools},\ \text{History},\ \text{Query})
\tag{31.4}\]
Like Lego: to change one piece, swap only that piece, and each piece has its own version number. Few-shot examples count against the budget too: the textbook suggests choosing only examples similar to the current question, within the \(M\) budget. Tool descriptions we wrote in EP06 Lab 1; what’s new here is including only the tools relevant to the task at hand, to save tokens and confuse the model less.

In Lab 4 we use LangChain’s SummarizationMiddleware (langchain==1.4.7) to do what we wrote ourselves in Lab 2:

Our code (Lab 2)
SummarizationMiddleware

SUMMARY_PROMPT

What the framework adds is checking the budget itself before every model call. But its default prompt wrote 410-token summaries that hit the cap, so it summarized again almost every turn. With our prompt from Lab 2, whose summaries stayed under 200 tokens, it summarized just once or twice and got all 6 papers. A framework saves code, but we need to know what it does inside.

title: Lab 1 — Count before you send
text:
1. Calling Gemma through OpenRouter
Why google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it — it follows instructions in Thai well, its tokenizer is open to download (we can count tokens on our machine exactly as the model does), and it can call tools, which Lab 4 needs
Why the provider is pinned to DeepInfra — the same one as EP03 and EP06 · it accepts a context of 262,144 tokens (this lab’s C) Providers accept different context sizes (some 131,072); without the pin, C would change whenever OpenRouter switches provider
Not free, but very cheap: DeepInfra charges USD 0.07 per million input tokens and USD 0.34 per million output tokens — at the end of the lab we add up the tokens actually used · The :free version doesn’t work (tested 2026-11-16: 3 out of 3 calls got 429 “rate-limited upstream”)
import json, os, random
from openai import OpenAI, BadRequestError

def load_key():
    try:  # Google Colab Secrets
        from google.colab import userdata
        return userdata.get("OPENROUTER_API_KEY")
    except ImportError:
        pass
    from dotenv import load_dotenv
    load_dotenv()
    return os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1", api_key=load_key())
MODEL = "google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it"
PROVIDER = {"order": ["deepinfra/fp8"], "allow_fallbacks": False}
EXTRA = {"reasoning": {"enabled": False}, "provider": PROVIDER}

USAGE = {"in": 0, "out": 0}

def chat(messages, **kw):
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(model=MODEL, messages=messages, max_tokens=300, extra_body=EXTRA | kw)
    USAGE["in"] += reply.usage.prompt_tokens
    USAGE["out"] += reply.usage.completion_tokens
    return reply

The API doesn’t count just the text — every message is wrapped in Gemma’s chat format (<|turn>user … <turn|>), and at the very end comes the header of the reply, <|turn>model, which the model continues So we count each message in that same format
def message_tokens(m):
    role = "model" if m["role"] == "assistant" else m["role"]
    return count_tokens(f"<|turn>{role}\n{m['content'].strip()}<turn|>\n")

REPLY_HEADER = count_tokens("<bos><|turn>model\n<|channel>thought\n<channel|>")

def count_messages(messages):
    return sum(message_tokens(m) for m in messages) + REPLY_HEADER

4. The pre-flight check (§18.2.6)
Before every LLM call:

Count the tokens of the assembled prompt with the model’s tokenizer
Compare with C − R (context size − space reserved for the answer)
If it’s over: compress, truncate, or stop with an explicit error
Log the token count of each part

The textbook’s fixed budget (Equation 18.2): S 10% · M 20% · T 10% · H 50% · R 10% of C

R = int(SHARE["R reserved"] * C)

class ContextOverflow(Exception):
    pass

def preflight(system, memory, tools, history, query):
    parts = {"S system": count_tokens(system), "M memory": count_tokens(memory), "T tools": count_tokens(tools),

    messages = assemble(system, memory, tools, history, query)
    total = count_messages(messages)

    print(f"  {'total':16} {total:>8,} / limit C - R = {C - R:,}")

def weight(m):

def importance(history, budget):

    for i in order:
        if used + message_tokens(history[i]) <= budget:
            keep.add(i)
            used += message_tokens(history[i])
    return [history[i] for i in sorted(keep)]

1. The model and token counting (from Lab 1)
Gemma 4 26B through OpenRouter, provider pinned to DeepInfra — why we chose the model and how to set up the key are in Lab 1 call calls the model at temperature 0 and records in CALLS which level of the tree each call is at and how many tokens it sent
import os, re, random
from openai import OpenAI
os.environ["HF_HUB_VERBOSITY"] = "error"
from tokenizers import Tokenizer

def load_key():
    try:  # Google Colab Secrets
        from google.colab import userdata
        return userdata.get("OPENROUTER_API_KEY")
    except ImportError:
        pass
    from dotenv import load_dotenv
    load_dotenv()
    return os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1", api_key=load_key())
MODEL = "google/gemma-4-26b-a4b-it"
EXTRA = {"reasoning": {"enabled": False}, "provider": {"order": ["deepinfra/fp8"], "allow_fallbacks": False}}
CALLS = []   # (depth, input tokens, output tokens) of every call

def call(prompt, depth=0):
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(model=MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}],
                                           max_tokens=500, temperature=0, extra_body=EXTRA)
    CALLS.append((depth, reply.usage.prompt_tokens, reply.usage.completion_tokens))
    return reply.choices[0].message.content

tok = Tokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL)

def count_tokens(text):
    return len(tok.encode(text, add_special_tokens=False).ids)

2. A document bigger than the budget
A research group’s meeting notes for a whole year (52 weeks · simulated data) — decisions about papers are spread over three places, and week 27 is a full meeting transcript, much longer than the other weeks
The question: which papers did the group decide to drop from the review’s main table, why, and in which week?
This lab’s budget per call: 1,500 tokens (kept small so the tree is easy to see — the same principle as a document of hundreds of thousands of tokens)
random.seed(3)  # simulated meeting notes, generated for teaching
PEOPLE = ["Nok", "Ton", "Ploy", "Bank", "Mint"]
TASKS = ["data loaders for the weather set", "the GPU booking sheet", "a reading list for new members", "plots for the seminar",
         "the baseline scripts", "the shared bibliography file", "unit tests for the metrics", "the poster draft"]
DECISIONS = {
    9:  "- Decision: drop P09 (Temporal Fusion Transformer) from the main table, because it was published in 2019, before our 2023 cutoff.",
    30: "- Ploy suggested dropping P05 (PatchTST), but we decided to keep it: it is the strongest baseline we have.",
    44: "- Decision: drop P08 (Chronos) from the main table, because its benchmark used a different forecast horizon, so the numbers are not comparable.",
}

def week(k):
    a, b = random.sample(PEOPLE, 2)
    lines = [f"## Week {k}", f"Present: {', '.join(random.sample(PEOPLE, 4))}."]
    for _ in range(5):
        lines.append(f"- {random.choice(PEOPLE)} worked on {random.choice(TASKS)}; about {random.randint(2, 9)} hours, "
                     f"{random.choice(['done', 'half done', 'blocked on data', 'needs review'])}.")
    lines.append(f"- Next week: {a} presents, {b} takes notes.")
    return "\n".join(lines)

def transcript(k):
    lines = [f"## Week {k} (full transcript of the review meeting)"]
    for i in range(60):
        lines.append(f"{random.choice(PEOPLE)}: On {random.choice(TASKS)}, I think we should spend {random.randint(1, 6)} more hours "
                     f"before the seminar, and check it with {random.choice(PEOPLE)} first.")
        if i % 6 == 5:
            lines.append("")
        if i == 33:
            lines.append("Nok: So we agree: drop P04 (Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?) from the main table, "
                         "because it is a critique of transformers, not a new model. It moves to the discussion section.")
    return "\n".join(lines)

weeks = []
for k in range(1, 53):
    w = transcript(k) if k == 27 else week(k)
    weeks.append(w + ("\n" + DECISIONS[k] if k in DECISIONS else ""))
DOC = "\n\n".join(["# Cogito Learn research group: meeting notes, 2026"] + weeks)
MAX = 1500
QUERY = ("Which papers did we decide to drop from the review's main table, and why? "
         "Answer one line per paper: paper id, week, reason.")
print(f"document: {count_tokens(DOC):,} tokens · budget per call: {MAX:,}")

def report(answer):
    print(answer)
    found = {}
    for p in ["P09", "P04", "P08"]:
        lines = [l for l in answer.splitlines() if p in l]
        if lines:
            weeks = re.findall(r"[Ww]eek (\d+)", lines[0])
            found[p] = "week " + weeks[0] if weeks else "week ?"
    print("→", found)

4. The textbook’s recursive_summarize

Base case: if the context fits the budget → call the model once
Recursive case: split by structure into chunks of at most half the budget → call itself on each chunk with a sub-question
Aggregate: join all the sub-results and ask the original question again

“Split by structure” for this document: by ## Week headings · if a single heading is still too big, by paragraphs

KEEP_HEADING = False

def split_by_structure(text, max_tokens):
    units, head = re.split(r"\n(?=## )", text), ""
    if len(units) == 1:              # a single section that is still too big → split it by paragraphs
        head, body = text.split("\n", 1)
        units = body.split("\n\n")

    chunks, cur = [], ""
    for u in units:
        if cur and count_tokens(cur + "\n\n" + u) > max_tokens:
            chunks.append(cur)
            cur = u
        else:
            cur = cur + "\n\n" + u if cur else u
    chunks.append(cur)
    if head and KEEP_HEADING:
        chunks = [head + "\n" + c for c in chunks]
    return chunks

def recursive_summarize(context, query, max_tokens, depth=0):
    n = count_tokens(context)
    print("    " * depth + f"depth {depth}: {n:,} tokens")
    if ___:

    chunks = split_by_structure(context, max_tokens // 2)
    sub_results = [recursive_summarize(c, f"Summarize this section relevant to: {query}", max_tokens, depth + 1)
                   for c in chunks]

    # ✏️ TODO 3 (▶ video 4:10): aggregate: join all the sub-results and ask the original question again

    combined = ___
    return call(f"Given these partial summaries, answer: {query}\n\nSummaries:\n{combined}", depth)

def recursive_summarize(context, query, max_tokens, depth=0):
    n = count_tokens(context)
    print("    " * depth + f"depth {depth}: {n:,} tokens")
    if n <= max_tokens:
        return call(f"{query}\n\nContext:\n{context}", depth)

    chunks = split_by_structure(context, max_tokens // 2)
    sub_results = [recursive_summarize(c, f"Summarize this section relevant to: {query}", max_tokens, depth + 1)
                   for c in chunks]

    combined = "\n---\n".join(sub_results)
    return call(f"Given these partial summaries, answer: {query}\n\nSummaries:\n{combined}", depth)

36  EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling

title: EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling
text:
Three things went wrong
Say we ask our research assistant to write a two-page report from three papers. The task has ten steps, and we see three things. First, it fetches the papers one at a time, waiting for the first before asking for the second. Second, at step seven the network drops for a moment, and it starts over from step one. Third, it runs the same search six times in a row. And at the end of the day, the API bill is longer than expected. None of these can be fixed inside the model, but the harness can prevent all of them.
In EP07 we covered the first kind of memory the harness manages, the context window. This episode covers the four topics the textbook takes next (Roitman 2026, sec. 18.4, §18.6–18.8): tools (§18.4), state (§18.6), errors (§18.7), and speed and cost (§18.8).
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
36  EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling

title: EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling
text:
Defining a tool
Before the model can call a tool, it has to know which tools exist, so the harness sends the tool definitions with every request. Each provider uses a slightly different format. OpenAI’s puts the arguments under parameters, Anthropic’s under input_schema; inside, both are the same JSON schema.
{"type": "function",
 "function": {"name": "get_paper",
              "description": "Get a paper's title and abstract by its id.",
              "parameters": {"type": "object",
                             "properties": {"paper_id": {"type": "string"}},
                             "required": ["paper_id"]}}}
When the model wants a tool, it replies with a request that carries an id. The harness runs the tool and sends the result back with the same id, like a cloakroom ticket: hand in the matching number to get the right coat back. When several tools run at once, the id is what tells which result belongs to which request. MCP is a common standard that frees us from any one provider’s format; it comes in full in EP13.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
36  EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling

title: EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling
text:
Who picks the tool
The model chooses, but the harness can shape the choice in three ways:



Table 36.1: Three ways to call tools










Mode
What happens
When




auto
the model decides whether to call a tool, and which
the default


forced
the harness makes the model call one specific tool
structured extraction


parallel
the model asks for several tools in one turn; the harness runs them concurrently
independent lookups






Parallel calls answer the first problem: ask for all three abstracts in one turn and wait only for the slowest, like ordering three dishes at once.
With hundreds or thousands of tools, putting every definition in the prompt wastes tokens and confuses the model. The textbook offers two ways: retrieve the few most relevant tools each turn, as Gorilla does over thousands of APIs (Patil et al. 2024), or train the model to pick better, like ToolLLM, trained on more than 16,000 APIs (Qin et al. 2024). In practice the two are combined.

In Lab 1: the model asked for three papers in a single message, each request with its own id. Running them one at a time took 4.5 s; all at once with ThreadPoolExecutor, 1.5 s, the time of the slowest one alone. Each result went back as a tool message with the id of its request.

title: EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling
section: Processing tool output in four steps
text:
Processing tool output in four steps
Raw tool output is rarely ready to go straight into the context. The textbook gives the harness four steps:

Parse and validate: check the output matches the expected format.
Truncate large outputs: web pages, code output or database results can be enormous. The textbook’s code cuts cheaply first, and asks a model to summarize only when the output is more than twice the budget. This is the \(T\) budget from EP07.
Normalize errors into one standard format, because every provider words errors differently, so the model can make sense of them.
Retry transient failures (a timeout, a rate limit) first, and only then report the failure to the model.


In Lab 1: run_tool checks the arguments before running anything. An unknown paper id P9 came back as {"error": "not_found", "detail": "no paper with id P9", "retry": false}, and the model told the user plainly that P9 wasn’t found. A simulated project page of 37,411 tokens was summarized down to the budget before going back to the model.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
36  EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling

title: EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling
text:
Sandboxes and prompt injection
The textbook calls tool execution a major attack surface. The harness must run tools in a sandbox isolated from the system (a container with no network), declare each tool’s permissions, limit CPU, memory and time, validate the arguments the model sends, and log every call.
The danger it stresses most is prompt injection through tool output (Greshake et al. 2023). Say the agent reads a paper’s web page, and the page hides a line telling it to ignore previous instructions. If the harness drops that text into the context as is, the model may follow it. So every tool output is data, not instructions: wrap it in tags the model is told to treat as data. Like a secretary reading a letter aloud to the boss: even if the letter says “secretary, transfer the money”, the secretary doesn’t do it.

In Lab 1: the simulated PatchTST page hid an instruction in an HTML comment telling AI assistants to end every answer with a fake download link. Unprotected, the model added the link in 5 of 8 runs. With the output wrapped in <tool_output> tags and a rule in the system prompt, 0 of 8. Wrapping lowers the risk; a real system still needs other guards too.

title: EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling
text:
Four layers of state
The textbook says agents are inherently stateful, and the harness manages four layers (Roitman 2026, sec. 18.6):



Table 36.2: Four layers of state










Layer
What it holds
Example




conversation
the history, every message with role, content and metadata
EP07’s history window


task
which subtasks are done, checkpoints, rollback
steps 1–3 of 6 done


agent
the current plan, pending tool calls, established facts
“the user’s timezone is UTC+9”


persistent
what lasts across sessions
user profiles, long-term memory (EP12)






A checkpoint is a saved snapshot of state that lets a task resume after a failure; rollback undoes the last few actions when a mistake is found. That answers the second problem: a drop at step seven shouldn’t mean starting over from step one.

In Lab 2: a six-step task (three paper notes, compare, title, report) with the network dropping at step four. Without a checkpoint it started over: 9 model calls for a task that needs 6. With a TaskState dataclass saved after every step (written to a temporary file, then swapped in with os.replace, so a crash mid-write can’t leave a broken file), it resumed at compare: 6 calls in total. Rolling back the last two steps to rewrite the opening paragraph for first-year students took 2 calls.

36  EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling

title: EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling
text:
Smarter retries
In EP06 we retried after one second, then two. The textbook gives the full formula: the wait before retry \(k\) is
\[
t_k \;=\; \min\!\big(2^k \cdot t_0 + U(0,\, t_0),\ t_{\max}\big)
\tag{36.1}\]
With \(t_0 = 1\) s the waits are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 s, then the ceiling: exponential backoff, like calling a friend whose line is busy and waiting longer each time. The random term \(U(0, t_0)\) is jitter: if ten agents sharing one key are all rate-limited at once and each waits exactly the same time, they all come back together and get limited again. Jitter spreads them out.
The textbook adds two more options: if the main model is unavailable, switch to a fallback model; if a tool is down, tell the model plainly and let it carry on without it (graceful degradation).

In Lab 3: a simulated search API refused three times with a 429. With \(t_0 = 0.5\) s the waits were 0.75, 1.28 and 2.40 s, and the fourth try answered. Without jitter, ten agents all came back at exactly 0.5 s; with jitter they spread out between 0.63 and 0.92 s. With the main model made unavailable, the harness tried it three times, then switched to Gemma 3 12B, which answered.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
36  EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling

title: EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling
text:
Detecting loops
The third problem: the agent calls the same tool with the same arguments again and again. The textbook gives three methods: a cap on the number of steps (which we’ve used since EP03, but by step fifty a lot is spent), hashing each action’s tool and arguments, and watching whether the state makes progress. With hashing, it’s a loop if two steps have the same hash no more than \(W\) steps apart:
\[
\exists\, i < j:\ h(a_i) = h(a_j) \ \wedge\ j - i \leq W
\tag{36.2}\]
Like pressing a lift button again and again when it’s already lit: repeating doesn’t change anything.
Some tasks really can’t be finished. A good agent then fails gracefully in four parts: what was accomplished, why it couldn’t continue, a way forward, and the state saved so the task can resume. To know what happened, the textbook’s three pillars are a trace of every run, logs with tokens, latency and cost, and metrics such as success rate and cost per task. We built a trace in EP06 Lab 2.

In Lab 3: a polling tool kept answering “the PDF is still being converted, call again”. With only a step cap, the agent made 12 model calls, all asking for the same thing. A LoopGuard that hashes each call over a window of 5 stopped it at the third identical request (3 calls), with a four-part message and the state saved to stuck_task.json.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
36  EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling

title: EP08 Tools, State and Error Handling
text:
Speed and cost
For speed the textbook gives four options: parallel tool calls, streaming, speculative execution (starting the likely next tool call early) and prompt caching. Every step of our task sends the same system prompt and tool definitions, so many providers keep the work already done on that repeated beginning; the textbook says the cached part gets 50–90% cheaper and faster. But the cache only works for a beginning that is exactly the same. Put the current time on the first line and the beginning differs every call. The rule: static first, changing last.
For cost, the textbook’s equation sums every model call and every tool call in a task:
\[
\text{Cost} \;=\; \sum_{i} \big(p_{\text{in}} \cdot n_{\text{in},i} + p_{\text{out}} \cdot n_{\text{out},i}\big) \;+\; \sum_{j} c_j
\tag{36.3}\]
So it recommends a token budget per task, a small cheap model for simple steps, and caching tool outputs that always give the same answer. When many agents share one key, it adds a shared rate limiter, priority queues and backpressure: reject new tasks plainly with a 503 when the queue is full, rather than queuing them forever.

In Lab 4: a system prompt of about 4,600 tokens and eight questions. With the static part first, the first call wasn’t cached but 5 of 8 were, and a cached call cost almost half as much. With the time on the system prompt’s first line, 0 of 8. Moving one line saved 27% of the total. Makora’s discount on cached tokens is about 46%, below the textbook’s 50–90%: it depends on the provider. Counting the tools too (simulated at $0.001 a call), the tools cost about three times the model. A TokenBudget of 20,000 tokens warned at question four and stopped the task at question five.

import json, os, time
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor
from openai import OpenAI

def load_key():

client = OpenAI(base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1", api_key=load_key())

PROVIDER = {"order": ["makora"], "allow_fallbacks": False}

    USAGE["out"] += reply.usage.completion_tokens

### Summary of PatchTST (2023) Project Page

**Core Methodology**
PatchTST is a time-series forecasting model that utilizes a "patching" mechanism. Instead of processing individual time steps, the model splits each series into **patches of 16 steps**. Additionally, the architecture is designed to handle each channel within a multivariate series independently.

**Performance Overview**
The provided data contains extensive error metrics across several datasets (ETTh1, ETTh2, ETTh3, and ETTh4) at various forecasting horizons (96, 192, 288, and 384). The results are reported using two primary error measurements:
*   **MSE** (Mean Squared Error)
*   **MAE** (Mean Absolute Error)

**Key Data Observations**
While the page contains a large volume of repetitive experimental results, the following patterns can be identified across the ETTh datasets:

*   **ETTh1 (Horizon 96):** MSE typically fluctuates between approximately **0.300 and 0.396**, with MAE ranging between **0.350 and 0.446**.
*   **ETTh2 (Horizon 192):** MSE typically fluctuates between approximately **0.301 and 0.397**, with MAE ranging between **0.351 and 0.447**.
*   **ETTh3 (Horizon 288):** MSE typically fluctuates between approximately **0.302 and 0.398**, with MAE ranging between **0.352 and 0.448**.
*   **ETTh4 (Horizon 384):** MSE typically fluctuates between approximately **0.303 and 0.399**, with MAE ranging between **0.353 and 0.449**.

The results demonstrate consistent performance levels across the various testing iterations provided in the dataset.

get_full_text simulates a tool whose PDF conversion never finishes: it answers "processing … Call again" every time. An agent with nothing to stop it calls the same request again and again until max_steps (our last-resort guard since EP03)

    "name": "get_full_text",
    "description": "Get the full text of a paper by id. The PDF is converted on demand; if it is not ready yet, call again.",
    "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"paper_id": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["paper_id"]}}}]

        messages.append(reply.model_dump(exclude_none=True))

                return graceful_failure(guard, messages)
            messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call.id, "content": json.dumps(get_full_text(**args))})

class LoopGuard:
    def __init__(self, window=5, k=3):

        h = hashlib.sha256(f"{tool}:{json.dumps(args, sort_keys=True)}".encode()).hexdigest()[:8]

RULES = ("You are the Cogito Learn research assistant.\n"
         "Rules: cite paper ids like [P12]; answer in under 60 words; say 'not in the catalog' if unsure.\n\n"

QUESTIONS = ["Which papers use patching?", "Name one anomaly detection paper.", "Which papers are from 2024?",

             "Which papers do frequency mixing?", "Name an MLP paper about forecasting."]
def ask(system, user):
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(model=MODEL, max_tokens=80, extra_body=EXTRA,
        messages=[{"role": "system", "content": system}, {"role": "user", "content": user}])
    return reply.usage

def run(name, build):
    total, hits = 0.0, 0
    for q in QUESTIONS:
        system, user = build(q)
        usage = ask(system, user)
        cost, cached = call_cost(usage)
        total += cost; hits += cached > 0
        print(f"  {usage.prompt_tokens:,} in · cached {cached:,} · ${cost:.6f}")
    print(f"{name}: {hits}/{len(QUESTIONS)} calls hit the cache · ${total:.5f}\n")
    return total

title: EP09 Building a Production Harness
text:
Parts on the garage floor
Over EP07 and EP08 we collected every part of the harness: the context budget, running tools, retries, catching an agent that loops, and checkpoints. But car parts laid out on the garage floor are not a car you can drive. This episode answers two questions: how do all these parts fit into one program, and once it’s built, how do we know it works before we hand it to anyone else?
The textbook answers the first with Listing 18.1, a complete harness in one Python file, and the second with five ways to test an agent (Roitman 2026, sec. 18.10). Our running example is the research assistant from EP07–EP08: it searches a small paper library, reads abstracts, and saves a report, but only after a person approves.

title: EP09 Building a Production Harness
text:
Listing 18.1: one file, five parts



Table 42.1: The parts of Listing 18.1









Part
Its job




Message · ToolDefinition
the two data types: one message in the conversation, and a tool’s ID card


ContextManager
a budget for every part of the context, trimming, and a check before each model call


ToolExecutor
runs tools without trusting them: approval, a time limit, retries, a cap on the output


LoopDetector
a fingerprint per action, to notice the agent repeating itself


AgentHarness
the ReAct loop that ties them together, with a run_id on every log line






A ToolDefinition has five fields. Three go to the model: name, description and the JSON schema of its parameters. Two the model never sees: the Python function that does the work (handler), and requires_approval, which says whether a person must say yes first.

title: EP09 Building a Production Harness
section: ContextManager: a budget on every message
text:
ContextManager: a budget on every message
The listing splits the context window into five shares:



Table 42.2: The context budget in Listing 18.1





Part
Share




system prompt
10%


memory
20%


tool definitions
10%


conversation history
50%


reserved for the answer
10%






Every time a message is added, the history is checked against its share. Over budget, the oldest message goes first, but the first message (the user’s question) always stays. And one detail matters a lot: if a dropped message asked for tools, every tool result that follows it must go too. A tool result left behind without its request makes the whole request invalid for the API. Before each model call, a preflight check adds up the system prompt, the tool definitions and the history and compares them with the window minus the reserved share.

In Lab 1 we counted tokens with Gemma’s own tokenizer instead of the listing’s tiktoken for GPT-4o, as the textbook’s summary says: count with the tokenizer of the model you actually use. In Lab 2 a unit test trimmed a small history and confirmed that what was left was the question, the later request and its result: the first request left together with both of its results.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
42  EP09 Building a Production Harness

title: EP09 Building a Production Harness
section: ToolExecutor: run tools without trusting them
text:
ToolExecutor: run tools without trusting them
Every tool request passes through four steps:

Unknown tool → an error message back to the model, not a crash.
Approval: if the tool requires_approval, ask a person first; if they say no, the model gets “Action rejected by human reviewer.” and finds another way.
Run with a time limit (30 s); on a timeout or an error, wait and try again, 1 s then 2 s, at most three attempts. The textbook puts retries at the tool level, because tools fail more often and usually recover on a second try.
Cap the output at 2,000 tokens, with a note saying it was cut.

Every way out is a text message back to the model; none of them crashes the program.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
42  EP09 Building a Production Harness

title: EP09 Building a Production Harness
text:
LoopDetector: a fingerprint per action
For every tool call, the detector takes an MD5 fingerprint of the tool’s name and its arguments (with sorted keys) and keeps the last five. The same fingerprint twice in that window → the run stops with a polite message.

In Lab 2 testing with broken inputs found three things in the book’s code. A reworded search (“time series transformer” vs “transformers for time series”) is not a loop, because one different character gives a different fingerprint, though the textbook says the check catches near-repeats too. The loop check runs after the tools, so a repeated save_report had already run twice before the detector stopped it. And half-finished JSON arguments crashed run(), because the loop check parses the arguments again without a try; we fixed it as SaferHarness.
crumbs: M2 · Harness: the agent's operating system
42  EP09 Building a Production Harness

title: EP09 Building a Production Harness
text:
AgentHarness.run: the whole ReAct loop






flowchart TD
  A[preflight check] --> B[call the model]
  B -->|asks for tools| C[run tools at once<br/>asyncio.gather]
  C --> D[loop check · add results]
  D --> A
  B -->|answers| E[done]






Each run gets a short run_id stamped on every log line, so one run can be followed through mixed logs. The tools a model asks for in one turn run at the same time with asyncio.gather. And there are three special exits, each a polite message: the context is full, the agent is stuck in a loop, or it reached 50 iterations.

In Lab 1 the research assistant searched, then asked for three read_paper calls in one turn: “3 tool(s) done in 1.5s”, not 4.5 s. It asked for approval before save_report, and finished in 4 rounds for about $0.0003. When we said no, in some runs the model asked again with the same arguments and the LoopDetector stopped it; in others it gave its summary in the chat instead.

section: Five ways to test an agent
text:
Five ways to test an agent
The textbook says testing agents is fundamentally different from testing ordinary software: the model doesn’t answer the same way every time. It suggests five strategies:



Table 42.3: Five ways to test an agent harness










Strategy
What it is
In this EP




① unit tests
each part checked on its own
Lab 2


② mock LLM
the whole harness against a stand-in that replies from a script
Lab 2


③ evaluation
tasks with known answers → a success rate
EP06 Lab 2


④ adversarial
broken inputs on purpose: bad JSON, a tool that hangs, a tool that fails
Lab 2


⑤ regression
replay past runs after a change and check nothing got worse
Lab 3







In Lab 2 the whole harness passed four checks against a mock LLM in under half a second, with no API key and no cost. A tool that always fails was tried three times (3 s), and one that hangs timed out three times (4.5 s), before the model got an error message; the program never crashed.

title: EP09 Building a Production Harness
text:
Prompts are code
One short line in the chapter summary: prompts should be version-controlled, tested, and assembled from components. One changed sentence in a system prompt can change the agent’s whole behaviour.

In Lab 3 the system prompt was built from part files (role · rules · cite · format), with an id made of the version and a hash of its text. Five real tasks were recorded with v1, which read the right papers but never cited one. Replayed with v2, which adds “Always cite paper ids like [P2].”, all five improved and nothing got worse, at about the same cost. A “cheaper” v3 that answers in one sentence cut output tokens by about a third, but two tasks regressed: one cited both papers in a single bracket, [P1, P4], which our checker didn’t count, and one answered without reading a paper at all. Reading the traces told a real regression from a checker that needed fixing, and in one of our runs v3 regressed only one task, so replay more than once before you decide.

title: EP09 Building a Production Harness
text:
Framework or build your own
The textbook compares the main frameworks (Roitman 2026, sec. 18.9) and gives a rule of thumb. Use a framework when you’re prototyping, when your use case fits its abstractions, or when you need to integrate many tools quickly. Build your own when you have strict latency or cost requirements, when the framework’s abstractions leak in ways that cause bugs, when you need fine-grained control over the context, or when the harness is what sets your product apart.



Table 42.4: Our harness next to LangChain









Our harness (Lab 1)
LangChain (Lab 4)




ToolDefinition
@tool (schema from type hints and the docstring)


approval callback
HumanInTheLoopMiddleware + a checkpointer, resumed with Command(resume=...)


retry + backoff
ToolRetryMiddleware


ContextManager
ContextEditingMiddleware (clears old tool results)


MAX_ITERATIONS
ModelCallLimitMiddleware


LoopDetector
— written ourselves with @wrap_tool_call







In Lab 4 LangChain made the same four model calls as our harness. Its default token count is an estimate that was off both ways (18 vs 14 tokens on an English sentence, 14 vs 24 on a short JSON), so we passed in Gemma’s tokenizer. With retry listed before loop_detector, reading the missing paper P9 was called a loop on the very first try, because the retry passed through our detector a second time; in the other order it tried three times and the model said P9 doesn’t exist. No line was wrong, only the order in the list.

One more thing both harnesses showed: after we rejected save_report, in some runs the model’s final answer said the report had been saved, though nothing was. So a harness should check the system’s real state, not take the model’s word for what it did.

class LoopDetector:
    def __init__(self, window: int = 5, max_repeats: int = 2):

class LoopDetector:
    def __init__(self, window: int = 5, max_repeats: int = 2):
        self.window = window
        self.max_repeats = max_repeats
        self.action_hashes: list[str] = []

    def record(self, tool_name: str, args: dict) -> bool:
        h = hashlib.md5(f"{tool_name}:{json.dumps(args, sort_keys=True)}".encode()).hexdigest()
        self.action_hashes.append(h)
        recent = self.action_hashes[-self.window:]
        if recent.count(h) >= self.max_repeats:
            logger.warning("Loop detected: %s called %d times", tool_name, recent.count(h))
            return True
        return False

class AgentHarness:
    MAX_ITERATIONS = 50

    def __init__(self, system_prompt: str, tools: list[ToolDefinition],
                 max_tokens: int = 256_000, approval_cb: Optional[Callable] = None):
        self.ctx_mgr = ContextManager(max_tokens)
        self.executor = ToolExecutor(tools, approval_cb)
        self.loop_det = LoopDetector()
        self.tools = tools
        self.ctx_mgr.system_msg = Message(Role.SYSTEM, system_prompt)
        self.usage = {"in": 0, "out": 0}

    async def run(self, user_input: str) -> str:
        run_id = hashlib.md5(f"{time.time()}:{user_input}".encode()).hexdigest()[:8]
        start_ts = time.monotonic()
        logger.info("[%s] Starting run: %s", run_id, user_input[:80])
        self.ctx_mgr.add_message(Message(Role.USER, user_input))
        tool_defs = [t.to_api_dict() for t in self.tools]
        tool_tokens = sum(count_tokens(json.dumps(t)) for t in tool_defs)
        msg = None

        for iteration in range(self.MAX_ITERATIONS):
            if not self.ctx_mgr.preflight_check(tool_tokens):
                logger.error("[%s] Context overflow at iter %d", run_id, iteration)
                return "I've run out of context space. Please start a new conversation."
            try:
                response = await client.chat.completions.create(
                    model=MODEL, messages=self.ctx_mgr.build_messages(),
                    tools=tool_defs or None, tool_choice="auto", temperature=0.0, extra_body=EXTRA)
            except Exception as exc:
                logger.error("[%s] LLM call failed: %s", run_id, exc)
                return f"I encountered an error: {exc}"
            self.usage["in"] += response.usage.prompt_tokens
            self.usage["out"] += response.usage.completion_tokens
            msg, finish = response.choices[0].message, response.choices[0].finish_reason
            self.ctx_mgr.add_message(Message(Role.ASSISTANT, msg.content or "",
                tool_calls=[tc.model_dump() for tc in msg.tool_calls] if msg.tool_calls else None))
            if finish == "stop" or not msg.tool_calls:
                logger.info("[%s] Done in %d iters, %.2fs", run_id, iteration + 1, time.monotonic() - start_ts)
                return msg.content or "Task complete."

            results = await self._execute_tool_calls(msg.tool_calls, run_id)
            for tc in msg.tool_calls:
                if self.loop_det.record(tc.function.name, json.loads(tc.function.arguments)):
                    return "I seem to be stuck in a loop. Please clarify your request."
            for tool_call_id, result in results.items():
                self.ctx_mgr.add_message(Message(Role.TOOL, result, tool_call_id=tool_call_id))

        logger.warning("[%s] Max iterations reached", run_id)
        return ("I reached the maximum number of steps without completing the task. "
                "Here is what I found so far: " + (msg.content or ""))

    async def _execute_tool_calls(self, tool_calls: list, run_id: str) -> dict[str, str]:
        tasks = {}
        for tc in tool_calls:
            try:
                args = json.loads(tc.function.arguments)
            except json.JSONDecodeError:
                args = {}
            logger.info("[%s] Tool call: %s(%s)", run_id, tc.function.name, args)
            tasks[tc.id] = self.executor.execute(tc.function.name, args)
        t0 = time.monotonic()
        results = await asyncio.gather(*tasks.values(), return_exceptions=True)
        logger.info("[%s] %d tool(s) done in %.1fs", run_id, len(tasks), time.monotonic() - t0)
        return {tid: (f"Error: {r}" if isinstance(r, Exception) else r)
                for tid, r in zip(tasks.keys(), results)}

LIBRARY = {
    "P1": ("Informer (2021)", "ProbSparse self-attention makes long-sequence time-series forecasting faster."),
    "P2": ("PatchTST (2023)", "Splits each series into patches of 16 steps; each channel is handled on its own."),
    "P3": ("TimesFM (2024)", "A decoder-only foundation model that forecasts new series zero-shot."),
    "P4": ("Autoformer (2021)", "Replaces attention with auto-correlation and decomposes trend and season."),
    "P5": ("DLinear (2023)", "A single linear layer that beats many transformers on long-term forecasting."),
    "P6": ("BERT (2019)", "Pre-trains a bidirectional transformer on text with masked language modelling."),
}
SAVED = {}  # the simulated disk
async def search_papers(query: str, max_results: int = 3) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
    words = [w.rstrip("s") for w in query.lower().replace("-", " ").split() if len(w) > 3]
    hits = [(pid, t) for pid, (t, a) in LIBRARY.items() if any(w in (t + " " + a).lower() for w in words)]
    return json.dumps([{"id": pid, "title": t} for pid, t in hits[:max_results]])

async def read_paper(paper_id: str) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(1.5)
    title, abstract = LIBRARY[paper_id]
    return json.dumps({"id": paper_id, "title": title, "abstract": abstract})

def save_report(filename: str, text: str) -> str:
    SAVED[filename] = text
    return f"saved {len(text)} characters to {filename}"

async def search_papers(query: str) -> str:

async def read_paper(paper_id: str) -> str:

async def broken_tool(x: str) -> str:
    raise ConnectionError("database is down")

async def slow_tool(x: str) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(10)
    return "too late"

def tools():

    return [ToolDefinition("search_papers", "", schema, search_papers),

            ToolDefinition("broken_tool", "", schema, broken_tool),

LIBRARY = {
    "P1": ("Informer (2021)", "ProbSparse self-attention makes long-sequence time-series forecasting faster."),
    "P2": ("PatchTST (2023)", "Splits each series into patches of 16 steps; each channel is handled on its own."),
    "P3": ("TimesFM (2024)", "A decoder-only foundation model that forecasts new series zero-shot."),
    "P4": ("Autoformer (2021)", "Replaces attention with auto-correlation and decomposes trend and season."),
    "P5": ("DLinear (2023)", "A single linear layer that beats many transformers on long-term forecasting."),
    "P6": ("BERT (2019)", "Pre-trains a bidirectional transformer on text with masked language modelling."),
}

async def search_papers(query: str, max_results: int = 3) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
    words = [w.rstrip("s") for w in query.lower().replace("-", " ").split() if len(w) > 3]
    hits = [(pid, t) for pid, (t, a) in LIBRARY.items() if any(w in (t + " " + a).lower() for w in words)]
    return json.dumps([{"id": pid, "title": t} for pid, t in hits[:max_results]])

async def read_paper(paper_id: str) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(1.5)
    title, abstract = LIBRARY[paper_id]
    return json.dumps({"id": paper_id, "title": title, "abstract": abstract})

TOOLS = [
    ToolDefinition("search_papers", "Search the paper library. Returns ids and titles.",
        {"type": "object", "properties": {"query": {"type": "string"},
         "max_results": {"type": "integer", "default": 3}}, "required": ["query"]}, search_papers),
    ToolDefinition("read_paper", "Read one paper's abstract by its id (P1, P2, ...).",
        {"type": "object", "properties": {"paper_id": {"type": "string"}}, "required": ["paper_id"]}, read_paper),
]

In Lab 1 we wrote ToolDefinition with its JSON schema by hand — @tool builds the schema from the type hints and the docstring. requires_approval moves into middleware (part 3)
LIBRARY = {
    "P1": ("Informer (2021)", "ProbSparse self-attention makes long-sequence time-series forecasting faster."),
    "P2": ("PatchTST (2023)", "Splits each series into patches of 16 steps; each channel is handled on its own."),
    "P3": ("TimesFM (2024)", "A decoder-only foundation model that forecasts new series zero-shot."),
    "P4": ("Autoformer (2021)", "Replaces attention with auto-correlation and decomposes trend and season."),
    "P5": ("DLinear (2023)", "A single linear layer that beats many transformers on long-term forecasting."),
    "P6": ("BERT (2019)", "Pre-trains a bidirectional transformer on text with masked language modelling."),
}
SAVED = {}  # the simulated disk
from langchain.tools import tool

@tool
async def search_papers(query: str, max_results: int = 3) -> str:
    """Search the paper library. Returns ids and titles."""
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)
    words = [w.rstrip("s") for w in query.lower().replace("-", " ").split() if len(w) > 3]
    hits = [(pid, t) for pid, (t, a) in LIBRARY.items() if any(w in (t + " " + a).lower() for w in words)]
    return json.dumps([{"id": pid, "title": t} for pid, t in hits[:max_results]])

@tool
async def read_paper(paper_id: str) -> str:
    """Read one paper's abstract by its id (P1, P2, ...)."""
    await asyncio.sleep(1.5)
    title, abstract = LIBRARY[paper_id]
    return json.dumps({"id": paper_id, "title": title, "abstract": abstract})

@tool
def save_report(filename: str, text: str) -> str:
    """Save a finished report to a file."""
    SAVED[filename] = text
    return f"saved {len(text)} characters to {filename}"

TOOLS = [search_papers, read_paper, save_report]

4. Assemble the agent and run it (approve ✅)
create_agent = the ReAct loop of AgentHarness.run · the checkpointer keeps the run’s state, so it can stop for approval and carry on · thread_id names the run, like run_id
from langchain.agents import create_agent
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver
from langgraph.types import Command

SYSTEM = ("You are a research assistant for a university course. Use the tools to find and read papers "
          "before answering. When you need several papers, request them all in the same turn. "
          "Always cite paper ids like [P2].")
TASK = ("Find papers on transformers for time-series forecasting, read the three most relevant ones, "
        "and save a short report to report.md.")

agent = create_agent(model, TOOLS, system_prompt=SYSTEM,
                     middleware=[approval, loop_detector, retry, limit, context],
                     checkpointer=InMemorySaver())

async def run(inp, config):
    async for step in agent.astream(inp, config, stream_mode="updates"):
        for node, update in step.items():
            if node == "__interrupt__":
                for req in update[0].value["action_requests"]:
                    print(f"🔒 approval needed: {req['name']}(filename={req['args'].get('filename')!r})")
                continue
            for m in (update or {}).get("messages", []):
                if getattr(m, "tool_calls", None) and node == "model":
                    print("model asks:", ", ".join(f"{c['name']}({c['args'].get('paper_id') or c['args'].get('query') or c['args'].get('filename')})" for c in m.tool_calls))
                elif m.type == "tool":
                    print(f"  {m.name} → {str(m.content)[:70]}")
                elif node == "model":
                    print("ANSWER:", m.content)

def usage(config) -> str:
    msgs = agent.get_state(config).values["messages"]
    u = [m.usage_metadata for m in msgs if getattr(m, "usage_metadata", None)]
    return f"{len(u)} model calls · {sum(x['input_tokens'] for x in u):,} in + {sum(x['output_tokens'] for x in u):,} out"
config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": str(uuid.uuid4())}}

await run({"messages": [{"role": "user", "content": TASK}]}, config)
print(f"\n⏸ paused · saved so far: {list(SAVED)}")

title: EP10 RAG Fundamentals
section: Three limits, two kinds of knowledge
text:
Three limits, two kinds of knowledge
A model stores its knowledge in its weights, compressed during training. The textbook names three limits that come with this (Roitman 2026, sec. 16.1):

Hallucination (EP02): asked beyond what it reliably knows, it still answers confidently.
Staleness: the training data has a cutoff date. Our textbook came out in 2026, after our model was trained.
Domain specificity: a general model has never seen your company’s documents, your university’s regulations or your code.

Knowledge in the weights is parametric; knowledge in documents outside the model is non-parametric. The textbook’s picture: a plain model is a scholar who memorized an enormous library but graduated years ago. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) gives that scholar a library card: look things up, cite the source, and admit when a reference needs checking instead of guessing from memory.

In Lab 1, asked without RAG which analogy the book uses to explain RAG, Gemma answered confidently: “an open-book exam”. The phrase is on no page of the book. With RAG it answered “the library card”, citing Doc 2, page 295.

title: EP10 RAG Fundamentals
text:
Embeddings and cosine similarity
An embedding model turns a text into a list of numbers that stands for its meaning; ours returns 4,096. Texts with similar meanings get vectors that point the same way. Cosine similarity measures how much two vectors point in the same direction, and top-k keeps the k chunks with the highest score for a question.

In Lab 1 car·automobile scored ≈ 0.95, but car·banana still scored ≈ 0.58, not zero. Unrelated texts often score fairly high, so what we really use is the order, not a single number.

Generation: answer only from the documents
Listing 16.1 gives a prompt with three rules: answer using only the provided context; if the context isn’t enough, say so explicitly; cite sources as [Doc n]. Each chunk in the prompt is labelled with its Doc number, its file and its page. “The documents don’t say” is not a failure: it is exactly what we want.

In Lab 1, asked for the capital of Australia, the model said the context doesn’t contain it, even though it knows the answer. Our library doesn’t mention Australia, so it didn’t answer from memory.

title: EP10 RAG Fundamentals
text:
Sparse, dense and hybrid retrieval
Sparse retrieval scores a chunk by the query’s words it contains, like the index at the back of a book. The most widely used is BM25: rare words weigh more, repeating a word helps but levels off, and very long chunks lose a little. It wins on error codes, proper nouns and rare or new terms, needs no GPU, and is easy to explain, but “car” won’t find “automobile”.
Dense retrieval uses embeddings (the textbook’s example is DPR, with one encoder for questions and one for passages). It finds meaning: ask how to split a long document, and it finds the chunk about chunking. At millions of chunks the search is approximate (for example with FAISS). Table 16.2 compares more methods; the cross-encoder is the most accurate but slow, so it re-ranks chunks already retrieved (EP11).
Hybrid uses both and merges the results. The two scores are on different scales, so the textbook uses Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which looks only at ranks:
\[\text{RRF}(d) = \sum_{\text{lists}} \frac{1}{60 + \text{rank}(d)}\]
Rank 3 in BM25 and rank 7 in dense gives 1/63 + 1/67 ≈ 0.0308; first in both gives ≈ 0.0328. The 60 keeps the top ranks from dominating.

In Lab 2 we wrote BM25 and RRF ourselves, and RRF matched the book’s 0.0308 and 0.0328. “What is PLAID?”: BM25 found it at rank 1, dense around rank 99. Asked about parent-child chunking in other words, dense found pages 302–303 and BM25 missed them. On 10 questions, hit@3 was BM25 4, dense 4, hybrid 8. Better overall, but not on every question: two got worse.

title: EP10 RAG Fundamentals
text:
Chunking
The textbook calls chunking one of the highest-impact decisions in a RAG system (Roitman 2026, sec. 16.4). A good chunk is small enough for the embedding model, about one topic, and makes sense on its own.

Fixed size with overlap: cut every W tokens, neighbours sharing O tokens, so a sentence cut at a boundary is whole in one of them. A 1,000-token document with W = 512 and O = 64 gives ⌈(1000 − 64) / (512 − 64)⌉ = 3 chunks (Equation 16.19).
Semantic: cut where neighbouring sentences stop being similar.
Structure-aware: split at headers, functions or classes, and never split a table mid-row.
Parent-child: search with small chunks (precise), but send the model the bigger chunk around the match (enough context).

2. Asking without RAG
The textbook came out in 2026, after Gemma was trained — does the model know this book?
question = ("In Roitman's book The Hitchhiker's Guide to Agentic AI, "
            "what analogy does the RAG chapter use to explain RAG?")

In Roitman's book *The Hitchhiker's Guide to Agentic AI*, the analogy used to explain **Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)** is that of an **open-book exam.**

Here is how the analogy breaks down:

*   **The LLM (Large Language Model) is the student:** The student has a vast amount of general knowledge and reasoning ability (the pre-training), but they might forget specific details, hallucinate facts, or lack access to information that was published after they finished studying.
*   **RAG is the textbook/reference material:** Instead of forcing the student to rely solely on their memory (parametric memory), RAG provides the student with a specific textbook or a set of notes (the external knowledge base) to look at during the exam.
*   **The Process:** When a question is asked, the "student" (LLM) first looks up the relevant passage in the "textbook" (Retrieval), reads it, and then uses their reasoning skills to write a perfect answer based on that specific information (Generation).

By using this analogy, Roitman illustrates that RAG doesn't change how "smart" the model is; rather, it changes what information the model has available to it at the moment it needs to answer a question.

from langchain_core.retrievers import BaseRetriever

def words(text):
    return re.findall(r"\w+", text.lower())

class OurBM25(BaseRetriever):
    docs: list
    k: int = 3

    def _get_relevant_documents(self, query, *, run_manager=None):
        bags = [Counter(words(d.page_content)) for d in self.docs]
        lens = [sum(bag.values()) for bag in bags]
        N, avgdl = len(bags), sum(lens) / len(bags)
        df = Counter(w for bag in bags for w in bag)
        k1, b = 1.5, 0.75
        scores = []
        for bag, dl in zip(bags, lens):
            s = 0.0
            for t in words(query):
                idf = math.log((N - df[t] + 0.5) / (df[t] + 0.5) + 1)
                s += idf * bag[t] * (k1 + 1) / (bag[t] + k1 * (1 - b + b * dl / avgdl))
            scores.append(s)
        best = np.argsort(-np.array(scores))[:self.k]
        return [self.docs[i] for i in best]

Q: What analogy does the textbook use to explain RAG? · pages [296, 295, 305]
A: The textbook uses "The Library Analogy" to explain RAG [Doc 2]. It compares a parametric LLM to a scholar who has memorized an enormous library but graduated years ago, while RAG provides that scholar with a library card, allowing them to look things up in real time, cite sources, and acknowledge when they need to check a reference instead of guessing from memory [Doc 2]. 

Q: How do I combine keyword search and embedding search? · pages [314, 303, 332]
A: Based on the provided documents, there is no information explaining how to combine keyword search and embedding search. The documents mention "Hybrid retrieval: dense similarity + temporal recency" [Doc 3] and "Dense + sparse + multi-vec" in relation to the BAAI/bge-m3 model [Doc 1], but they do not provide instructions on combining keyword search with embedding search.

Q: What analogy does the textbook use to explain RAG? · pages [305, 296, 307]
A: The provided text does not contain an analogy used to explain RAG. It does, however, state that "Fine-tuning teaches the model how to reason and respond; RAG provides what to reason about" [Doc 2]. 

Q: How do I combine keyword search and embedding search? · pages [298, 311, 301]
A: You can combine keyword search (sparse scores) and embedding search (dense scores) using the following methods:

*   **Linear Combination:** A simple way to combine them is through a linear combination of the scores: $s_{hybrid}(d,q) = \alpha \cdot s_{dense}(d,q) + (1-\alpha) \cdot s_{sparse}(d,q)$ [Doc 1].
*   **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF):** Because scores from different systems are not directly comparable, RRF can be used to combine results by operating on ranks rather than scores [Doc 1]. The formula is $RRF(d) = \sum_{r \in R} \frac{1}{k + rank_r(d)}$, where $R$ is the set of ranked lists (such as BM25 ranking and dense ranking) [Doc 1].

section: The question we still can’t find
text:
The question we still can’t find
In EP10, one question missed with every method: which analogy does the RAG chapter of Roitman’s The Hitchhiker’s Guide to Agentic AI use to explain RAG? With the author’s name and the book’s title in it, the library-card chunk sat at rank 8 with dense search, 5 with hybrid and 17 with parent-child. This episode tries two things: transform the question before searching, and let an agent decide what to search, where, and whether it has found enough. Then the key question: how do we measure whether RAG really got better?
crumbs: M3 · Knowledge: RAG
52  EP11 Advanced & Agentic RAG

title: EP11 Advanced & Agentic RAG
text:
Before retrieval: transform the question
User questions are often ambiguous, too short, or worded differently from the documents (Roitman 2026, sec. 16.5.1).

HyDE: have the model write a hypothetical answer, and embed that instead of the question. The draft may be wrong: we only search with it, we don’t answer with it. Written like the documents, it lands closer to the right chunk (Equation 16.20).
Step-back: ask a broader question first. For the boiling point of ethanol at 2 atm, also search what affects the boiling point of liquids.
Multi-query: rewrite the question several ways, search for each, merge the results.
RAG-Fusion: multi-query plus the original, all ranked lists merged with RRF (Listing 16.8), the formula from EP10 Lab 2. A chunk that ranks well for many queries rises to the top.


In Lab 1 HyDE’s draft said the book uses an “open-book exam”, which is wrong, yet searching with it put the library-card chunk at rank 1. Plain multi-query kept the book’s title in every variant (ranks 12, 13 and 9; fused: 9); told to leave out titles and author names, the fused result was rank 1.
crumbs: M3 · Knowledge: RAG
52  EP11 Advanced & Agentic RAG

title: EP11 Advanced & Agentic RAG
text:
After retrieval: re-rank and compress
The retriever from EP10 encodes questions and documents separately, so document embeddings are computed ahead of time and search is fast. A cross-encoder reads the question and a document together in one pass: much more accurate, but slow, and it can’t do the first search because there is nothing to store in advance. So it re-ranks only the chunks already retrieved, typically 20 to 100 (Roitman 2026, sec. 16.5.2). Like hiring: screen résumés by keyword first, then interview five people. Contextual compression then cuts each chunk down to the part that answers the question.

In Lab 1 the cross-encoder put the library-card chunk at rank 1 with a score of 0.996; the next chunk scored 0.50. On 20 test questions, hit@3: dense 12 · HyDE 16 · RAG-Fusion 14 · re-rank 18 · HyDE + re-rank 19.

title: EP11 Advanced & Agentic RAG
section: RAG that checks itself, and two more patterns
text:
RAG that checks itself, and two more patterns

Self-RAG trains one model to decide whether to retrieve, whether what it got is relevant, whether its answer is supported and whether it is useful, through four special tokens learned in training.
CRAG keeps the model and adds an evaluator that grades each document correct, ambiguous or incorrect: some correct → strip the irrelevant sentences and answer from the rest; all incorrect or ambiguous → fall back to web search.
Adaptive RAG sorts questions by difficulty with a small classifier: no retrieval, one retrieval, or several rounds.
Graph RAG extracts entities and relations into a graph, finds communities and summarizes each. It excels at global questions (the main themes of a corpus) but is expensive to build; for local questions standard RAG is still better.

title: EP11 Advanced & Agentic RAG
text:
Agentic RAG
Static RAG retrieves once, then answers. The textbook lists where it fails: multi-hop questions (“who founded the company that acquired OpenAI’s main competitor in 2023?”), ambiguous questions, sub-questions that need different knowledge bases, and a first search that shows a different query is needed (Roitman 2026, sec. 16.7). Agentic RAG treats retrieval as a sequence of decisions: the state is the question and the documents found so far; the actions are retrieve, reason, generate or stop; the reward is a correct answer. Like ReAct in EP05, with search as the main tool.

Routing across sources



Table 52.1: Three ways to route a question to a knowledge source (Listing 16.9 uses the LLM)





Way to route
